primary_sources: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), Chapter 9

stimulus.text: “Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us. It eluded us then, but that's no matter — tomorrow we will run faster, stretch out our arms farther. . . . And one fine morning — / So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.” — F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), Chapter 9. Verbatim excerpt, public domain.
stimulus.source_note: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), Chapter 9. Verbatim excerpt, public domain (published 1925).

source: original; stimulus verbatim from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), Chapter 9, public domain
stem: The passage best shows Fitzgerald's view that wealthy Americans of the 1920s

options.text: had found lasting happiness and purpose in their riches
options.misconception: Gatsby's dream 'eluded' him and the future 'recedes.' Lasting happiness is exactly what the passage denies.

options.text: had turned away from material goods and wealth entirely
options.misconception: Gatsby chases the green light, a dream of wealth and Daisy. He never turns away from material goods.

options.text: had solved the problems of the past for good
options.misconception: The past pulls them back 'ceaselessly.' Problems solved for good would not keep pulling.

options.text: chased a receding future while the past pulled them back

rationales.A: Gatsby's dream 'eluded' him and the future 'recedes.' Lasting happiness is exactly what the passage denies.
rationales.B: Gatsby chases the green light, a dream of wealth and Daisy. He never turns away from material goods.
rationales.C: The past pulls them back 'ceaselessly.' Problems solved for good would not keep pulling.
rationales.D: Background from the books: The Great Gatsby exposed the shallowness of the wealthy, whose pursuit of the future kept receding while the past dragged them back. The boats row forward and drift backward at once.
rationales.general:
1. Read the future in the passage: it 'recedes before us' and 'eluded us.'
2. Read the past: the boats are 'borne back ceaselessly into the past.'
3. Ask what the two motions add up to: striving forward while being pulled back.
4. Name Fitzgerald's view: the rich chased a future they could not reach.
Remember: when a passage gives you two opposite motions, the meaning sits in the tension between them.
